transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-07-08
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (ScalePay Eng Manager), Maria Gomez (ScalePay ML Engineer), Samir Patel (ScalePay SRE)

Summary: Weekly POC check-in focusing on SDK integration, tool/function calling behavior, structured output (JSON schema), and performance tuning. Action items captured at end.

Topics: SDK usage, function/tool call auth patterns, structured output parsing, latency/cost tradeoffs, next steps.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're on the weekly POC sync for ScalePay, I think we've got, like, 45 minutes, we'll go through results and next steps. Priya, you wanna kick off with the SDK notes?
[00:18] Priya Nair: yeah sure, thanks Alex. So last week we shipped the updated SDK that supports function calling and structured output helpers, there's a sample snippet in the repo. couple of notes: we saw one integration issue around the default timeout, so the SDK was aborting on long-running tool calls, and also the JSON schema validation was sometimes failing when clients returned extra fields.
[00:38] Jordan Lee: yeah that was our team, we hit the timeout when the payment-lookup tool did a remote DB join, it took 6.5s and the SDK aborted at 5s. we increased the timeout locally and it helped but want to understand recommended defaults.
[00:52] Priya Nair: default is conservative for hosted mode to prevent runaway tokens; recommendation is to set functionTimeoutMs to 15_000 for payment lookups or use async tool call pattern, we can add a retry/backoff in SDK as well.
[01:06] Maria Gomez: also on structured output, the model occasionally emits the amount field as a string instead of number, which breaks our downstream schema validation. is there a way to enforce stricter types from the model side?
[01:20] Priya Nair: yeah, so we provide a structured_output schema that the runtime uses for validation and post-processing. but model output isn't always deterministic; we recommend using the SDK's sanitize_and_cast helper which will coerce types and raise a soft warning for mismatches. we'll share an example JSON Schema.
[01:36] Samir Patel: quick infra question: if we move to dedicated or private, does that change the SDK config? or is it same surface?
[01:44] Alex Kim: same surface, the SDK is environment-agnostic—just swap the endpoint and API key. for private deployments you can point it at the private control plane, and there's an extra flag for KMS key id for encrypting cached payloads.
[01:58] Jordan Lee: awesome. ok can we deep dive into the benchmark numbers you sent? the spreadsheet showed p50 ~120ms token time which seems optimistic compared to our local tests.
[02:09] Priya Nair: sure, the numbers in the sheet are for our curated smaller context model with quantization, and they assumed continuous KV cache hits. if you run cold starts or longer contexts p95 moves up. what was your test scenario?
[02:22] Jordan Lee: we ran a 2k token prompt, no prefix cache, single request per second, p95 was around 850ms end-to-end including network.
[02:33] Priya Nair: that aligns—our p95 for that config is 700–900ms depending on sequence length. we recommended batching for synchronous workloads or using dedicated pool for consistent p95.
[02:45] Alex Kim: and to call out cost tradeoffs, batching reduces per-token cost but can increase tail latency; dedicated reduces variability but has commit costs.
[02:55] Maria Gomez: regarding function calls—we tried two approaches: inline function call where the model emits a tool invocation and synchronous call to our microservice, and the other using Redwood tool bridge where Redwood proxies authenticated requests. any advice?
[03:10] Priya Nair: both are valid. if you want consistent auth and VPC control, the tool bridge with short-lived credentials is easier. inline gives you lower hop-count but you need to manage auth and retries in your service. we also have an example for using signed JWTs for calls through the bridge.
[03:26] Samir Patel: is the bridge compatible with our egress restrictions? we need to avoid broad outbound to internet, prefer peered endpoints.
[03:34] Alex Kim: yes, for private/Dedicated we support VPC peering and private endpoints. Samir, we flagged an action to confirm peering window.
[03:43] Jordan Lee: thanks. one more note: the SDK logs were a bit noisy in our staging app, showing repeated error messages when the schema sanitizer coerced types. can we make that adjustable?
[03:55] Priya Nair: absolutely, there's a log_level in SDK config, set to warn or error to suppress soft warnings. we'll send a snippet.
[04:03] Alex Kim: ok we'll capture those items. moving on, Maria you ran the structured-output QA run—what were the failure modes?
[04:12] Maria Gomez: yes, ran 500 sample prompts through the structured-output pipeline. about 12% failed strict schema validation: mostly type mismatches (string vs number), occasionally missing required fields, and a handful of cases where the model returned an array for a field we expected scalar. also there were a few cases where model used synonyms for enums, like 'card' vs 'credit_card'.
[04:33] Priya Nair: for enums we recommend canonicalization rules in the post-processor (map synonyms). the sanitize_and_cast helper supports enum maps and will tag low-confidence casts.
[04:44] Jordan Lee: do you have recommended prompt templates to reduce these mismatches? we tried to add explicit type annotations in the system prompt but results varied.
[04:53] Priya Nair: include an explicit schema in the system prompt and an example output block; also use the structured_output enforcement flag which injects stronger constraints. still not 100% deterministic but reduces failures to sub-5% for many workloads. we'll share the template.
[05:08] Alex Kim: quick note—we updated the SDK to support a strict_mode boolean that will force the call to fail when schema validation fails so you can catch issues earlier. that's off by default for flexibility.
[05:19] Maria Gomez: that's helpful for unit tests. ok on performance tuning—we saw token cost on your sheet seemed lower than our run. can we reconcile tokenization differences?
[05:29] Priya Nair: token counts depend on tokenizer and pre-tokenization steps; if you pass binary attachments or certain whitespace it's counted differently. we recommend using our token_count helper in SDK to normalize. also model variations and quantization profiles change effective token emission.
[05:45] Jordan Lee: cool. about retries and idempotency—if a function call times out and we retry, how do you recommend deduping? we don't want double charges or duplicate processing.
[05:56] Priya Nair: pass a client_request_id in the SDK function call wrapper; the runtime will attach that to logs and the function bridge will forward it so your service can dedupe. we'll add that to the snippet.
[06:08] Samir Patel: security question—what's the audit trail for tool calls? we need per-request logs for SOC2.
[06:16] Alex Kim: audit logs are available in the console and can be shipped to your SIEM; for private deployments logs can be sent to your own logging endpoint, and we support redaction rules. we'll share SOC2 appendix.
[06:28] Jordan Lee: great. can we talk about the proposed canary next week? we want to do a small canary on production checkout flow using the SDK in app-server. what's the recommended rollout rate?
[06:39] Priya Nair: start with 1% traffic, validate success metrics for 48 hours (error rate <0.1%, latency within threshold), then 5%, 10% over a week. if dedicated, you can reserve burst capacity.
[06:52] Maria Gomez: what success metrics should we monitor for structured output? we care about schema pass rate, false positives in canonicalization, downstream processing errors.
[07:02] Priya Nair: schema pass rate, sanitized_cast_count, and a model_confidence_score if available. Redwood Console can emit those as per-route metrics; we can add a lightweight eval hook to push alerts.
[07:13] Alex Kim: ok good. any blockers from ScalePay side? Jordan?
[07:17] Jordan Lee: main blockers: finalize JSON Schema, fix SDK timeout/retry defaults, and infra peering window. once those are done we can run the canary.
[07:26] Alex Kim: sounds good. Priya, can you summarize what you'll send?
[07:30] Priya Nair: yes: (1) updated SDK snippet with functionTimeoutMs and client_request_id + retry/backoff example, (2) JSON Schema for structured output with sample unit tests, (3) prompt template for better determinism, (4) logging config options and link to SOC2 docs.
[07:46] Jordan Lee: perfect. also please include the token_count helper usage example so we can reconcile numbers.
[07:52] Priya Nair: will do.
[07:54] Maria Gomez: tiny follow-up—for the sanitize helper, will it ever mutate business-critical fields like transaction_id? we need to preserve IDs exactly.
[08:02] Priya Nair: sanitize_by_default won't mutate fields marked as immutable in the schema; mark transaction_id as immutable and it will only validate, not coerce. we'll show that in example tests.
[08:12] Samir Patel: network: I'll confirm peering, but if the peering has to wait we'll run the canary via a dedicated hosted pool first.
[08:20] Alex Kim: okay, that covers most. quick recaps and owners.
[08:24] Alex Kim: Recap — Alex will send pricing/practice notes? (laughter) no, Alex will share the standard canary checklist and pricing note. Priya sends SDK + schema + examples. Jordan runs end-to-end bench. Samir confirms peering.
[08:38] Jordan Lee: timeline looks good. let's tentatively schedule next sync same time next week, 7/15.
[08:45] Alex Kim: yep, I'll send calendar invite. thanks everyone.
[08:48] Maria Gomez: thanks, bye.
[08:50] Priya Nair: bye.
